row.basis: Joseph in prison; grapes pressed into Pharaoh’s cup
row.note: The commentary joins Joseph’s confinement to pressing; in Joseph’s prison story the cupbearer dreams of squeezing grapes into Pharaoh’s cup, while the dream belongs to the cupbearer.

row.basis: Joseph stores the abundant harvest
row.note: The commentary’s Yusuf year makes relief follow scarcity; Genesis has Joseph gather the abundant years’ produce into storehouses so the later famine can be survived.

row.basis: Joseph fettered
row.note: The commentary pairs Joseph’s imprisonment with patience; the psalm retelling puts his feet in fetters and his neck in iron, making confinement part of the Joseph story.

row.basis: Joseph tested while awaiting the promise
row.note: The commentary makes patience meet detention; the next line of the psalm says the Lord’s word tested Joseph until its fulfillment, giving his confinement a waiting-for-release dimension.

row.basis: Stored harvest interrupted by death
row.note: The commentary’s aged gardener loses the yield before enjoying it; Jesus’ rich farmer plans many years around his abundant stores, then is told that his life ends that night.

row.basis: Merchants’ wealth lost in one hour
row.note: The commentary compresses accumulated produce and capital into sudden loss; Revelation says Babylon’s great wealth is laid waste in one hour, as merchants watch their trade collapse.

row.basis: Crop, rain, and patience
row.note: The commentary joins rain, fruit, and sabr; James tells the farmer to wait patiently for the precious crop until it receives the early and late rains, making delay before yield the point.

row.basis: Life flourishes, then withers at evening
row.note: The commentary reads asr as the evening of a life; the psalm compares human flourishing to grass that sprouts in the morning and withers by evening.

row.basis: Brief lifespan and toil
row.note: The commentary makes a lifetime’s yield vulnerable at its late hour; the psalm counts human years as short and full of toil, then quickly gone.

row.basis: Light and rain clouds dim before old age
row.note: The commentary layers life’s late afternoon with rain and its destructive turn; Ecclesiastes pictures sun, moon, and stars darkening and clouds returning after rain in its approach to death.

row.basis: Fruit still borne in old age
row.note: The commentary’s old owner loses his garden as age advances; the psalm instead pictures the righteous still bearing fruit in old age, a concrete counter-image of fruitful late life.

row.basis: Short day, much work, pressing master
row.note: The commentary treats time as expiring capital and deeds as urgent; Tarfon says the day is short, the work abundant, and the Master of the House presses, joining time, labor, and accountability.

row.basis: Do not desist from unfinished work
row.note: The commentary’s closing community keeps transmitting good action within limited time; Tarfon says one need not finish the work but is not free to desist, adding persistence without claiming control of the outcome.

row.basis: Good deeds as fruit and principal
row.note: The commentary makes good works the lasting yield of time; Peah says certain deeds bear fruit in this world while their principal remains for the world to come, an explicit investment image.

row.basis: Release the bound and break the yoke
row.note: The commentary defines the steep ascent through freeing a captive; Isaiah’s fast is to loose wicked bonds, undo the yoke, and let the oppressed go free.

row.basis: Give bread to the hungry
row.note: The commentary names feeding on a day of hunger as part of the ascent; Isaiah places sharing bread with the hungry in the same account of true fasting.

row.basis: Lift an enemy’s overloaded donkey
row.note: The commentary moves from struggle toward companionship and mentions a beast of burden; Torah commands helping even an enemy’s donkey rise under its load, making cooperation concrete.

row.basis: A wounded traveler carried on an animal
row.note: The commentary’s road and burden imagery turns toward care; the Samaritan binds the robbed traveler’s wounds and places him on his own animal, converting a dangerous road encounter into help.

row.basis: Feed the hungry
row.note: The commentary makes feeding the hungry part of the difficult ascent; in Jesus’ judgment scene, feeding the hungry is named as a deed by which people answer the king.

row.basis: Visit the imprisoned
row.note: The commentary pairs release from captivity with feeding; Jesus’ judgment scene separately names visiting a person in prison, connecting practical care to final reckoning.

row.basis: Feed an enemy
row.note: The commentary’s movement from enmity to fellowship has a concrete ethic in Paul’s instruction to feed a hungry enemy, answering hostility with care.

row.basis: Bear one another’s burdens
row.note: The commentary turns from the isolated person to mutual counsel; Paul tells the community to carry one another’s burdens, making shared endurance an enacted duty.

row.basis: A companion lifts the fallen
row.note: The commentary’s steep path and transition into togetherness meet Ecclesiastes’ image of one companion raising another who falls on the road of life.

row.basis: A cord holds companions together
row.note: The commentary reads holding together as rescue from danger; Ecclesiastes says a three-strand cord is not quickly broken, giving the communal bond a material image.

row.basis: Two or three witnesses establish a matter
row.note: The commentary’s deathbed bequest depends on witnesses; Deuteronomy likewise rejects a single witness and requires two or three for a charge.

row.basis: Witness called under oath
row.note: The commentary gathers oath, testimony, and truth at the moment of a bequest; Leviticus treats hearing a public oath and withholding testimony as a legal offense.

row.basis: Death activates a will or covenant
row.note: The commentary’s death-triggered bequest meets Hebrews’ use of Greek diathēkē as a will: the writer uses the testator’s death to explain how the covenant takes effect.

row.basis: Signed deed, witnesses, and weighed silver
row.note: The commentary says the debt scene joins market and trust; Jeremiah records a land purchase with a signed deed, witnesses, and silver weighed out, a close transactional analogue.

row.basis: Sealed deeds kept in an earthen vessel
row.note: The commentary joins financial trust to preserved contents; Jeremiah orders sealed and open copies of the deed stored in a jar so they last, showing custody protecting a transaction.

row.basis: Promise and honesty in lending
row.note: The commentary brings debt together with trust; Sirach tells a lender to keep a promise and deal faithfully with the borrower, making reliability part of credit.

row.basis: Faithful business dealings at judgment
row.note: The commentary joins market trust to the day when deeds are faced; the Talmud’s first judgment question is whether one dealt faithfully in business.

row.basis: Faithfulness with wealth and entrusted riches
row.note: The commentary’s debt verse brings commerce and trust together; Jesus asks who will entrust true riches to someone unfaithful with worldly wealth.

row.basis: Another’s debt charged to Paul
row.note: The commentary’s testament and debt scenes make obligation transferable; Paul tells Philemon to charge any debt or wrong by Onesimus to him.

row.basis: A written promise to repay
row.note: The commentary joins a financial obligation to trust; Paul says he writes in his own hand that he will repay, turning personal assurance into a written pledge.

row.basis: A friend’s wounds can be faithful
row.note: The commentary lets truth be a straight, painful blow; Proverbs says a friend’s wounds may be trusted, presenting frank correction as a form of loyalty.

row.basis: Speak truth to one another
row.note: The commentary’s mutual counsel is centered on truth; Zechariah commands neighbors to speak truth and render judgments that make for peace.

row.basis: Truth spoken among interdependent members
row.note: The commentary turns truth into reciprocal counsel within a community; Paul says to speak truth with one’s neighbor because members belong to one another.

row.basis: Entrusted teaching passed to further teachers
row.note: The commentary ends with truth and patience changing hands; Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he heard to faithful people able to teach others, an explicit chain of transmission.

row.basis: Encourage the weak and be patient with all
row.note: The commentary’s community counsels patience; Paul joins encouraging the fainthearted and helping the weak to the instruction to be patient with everyone.

row.basis: Provoke one another to good works
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel issue in righteous action; Hebrews says to consider how to spur one another toward love and good works.

row.basis: The Day tests each person’s work
row.note: The commentary imagines deeds fitting like building material and truth as the day of reckoning; Paul says the Day reveals each builder’s work and fire tests it.

row.basis: People built together as living stones
row.note: The commentary pictures righteous action as bricks set in place; Peter calls believers living stones being built into a spiritual house, making the community itself constructed.

row.basis: Each part builds the whole body
row.note: The commentary’s believers add to one another; Paul’s body is joined through each supporting part and builds itself up in love.

row.basis: Members care for one another
row.note: The commentary’s mutual counsel makes the group interdependent; Paul says the body’s members should have the same care for one another.

row.basis: Patience as rule over oneself
row.note: The commentary reads sabr as self-restraint; Proverbs says ruling one’s spirit is greater than taking a city, making inner restraint the achievement.

row.basis: Patience in adversity
row.note: The commentary treats patience as something retained through hardship; Sirach tells the faithful to accept what befalls them and be patient in humiliation.

row.basis: Faithfulness tested like gold in fire
row.note: The commentary’s patience has a bitter, fiery trial aspect; Sirach says the faithful are tested in the furnace of humiliation as gold is tested in fire.

row.basis: Faithfulness chosen despite the furnace
row.note: The commentary calls condemned people’s readiness for fire a perverse patience; Daniel’s three youths accept the possibility of fire rather than worship another god, reversing what endurance serves.

row.basis: Every deed brought into judgment
row.note: The commentary says the day makes each person face their work; Ecclesiastes says every deed, including what is hidden, comes into judgment.

row.basis: Weighed and found wanting
row.note: The commentary links severed kinship to scales that come up light; Daniel’s wall-writing scene weighs a king and finds him wanting, making weight a verdict on conduct.

row.basis: Righteousness cannot be transferred to a child
row.note: The commentary places severed kinship beside individual weighing; Ezekiel says even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves, not sons or daughters, so family ties do not transfer standing.

row.basis: Each repaid according to deeds
row.note: The commentary says the day confronts everyone with their work; Paul states that God repays each person according to deeds.

row.basis: The dead judged by recorded deeds
row.note: The commentary joins the loss of kinship with personal weighing; Revelation depicts the dead judged from books according to what they had done.

row.basis: A seemingly right road ends in death
row.note: The commentary describes the human as straying within time; Proverbs warns that a way can seem right yet end in death, specifying the danger of misjudgment.

row.basis: Profit that costs one’s life
row.note: The commentary describes human life as capital that can melt into loss; Jesus asks what is gained by acquiring the whole world if one forfeits oneself.

row.basis: A year of trade and expected profit
row.note: The commentary treats time as capital; James depicts merchants planning a year in a city to trade and make profit, exposing life’s plans to uncertainty.

row.basis: Life as a passing mist
row.note: The commentary reads the time of a human life as brief and vulnerable; James calls life a vapor that appears briefly and then vanishes.

row.basis: Patient good work bears a later harvest
row.note: The commentary closes with deeds and patience transmitted together; Paul urges persistence in doing good because a harvest comes in its season if people do not give up.

row.basis: Self-control and endurance after faith
row.note: The commentary’s believers join faith to good action and sabr; Peter’s sequence adds self-control and endurance to faith-informed virtue.

row.basis: Faithful community defined by endurance
row.note: The commentary gathers belief, right action, and patience in a community; Revelation names the saints’ endurance together with keeping God’s commands and faith in Jesus.

row.basis: The world’s form is passing away
row.note: The commentary treats time and worldly capital as expiring; Paul tells believers to use the world without clinging to it because its present form is passing.

row.basis: Earthly treasure can be destroyed or stolen
row.note: The commentary’s accumulated fruit and capital remain vulnerable; Jesus warns that earthly stores are exposed to moth, corrosion, and thieves.

row.basis: Vineyard, grapes, and winepress
row.note: The commentary’s garden contains grapes and fruit meant for pressing; Isaiah’s cultivated vineyard has a winepress prepared for its expected grapes, though its yield proves different.

row.basis: A vineyard ruined when rain is withheld
row.note: The commentary’s garden is destroyed by a sudden storm after fruitfulness; Isaiah instead makes a failed vineyard waste and withholds rain, a distinct judgment pattern.

row.basis: A violent wind destroys a house amid accumulated loss
row.note: The commentary makes a whirlwind erase what was gathered; Job’s children die when a great wind collapses the house during their feast, after earlier losses of property.

row.basis: Wages vanish into a bag with holes
row.note: The commentary says human capital melts away; Haggai pictures earned wages disappearing into a bag with holes, tying loss to futile labor.

row.basis: Wealth perishes in a bad venture
row.note: The commentary’s garden loses its accumulated yield at the moment of expectation; Ecclesiastes describes wealth kept to its owner’s hurt and lost through a disastrous venture.

row.basis: Wealth grows wings and flies away
row.note: The commentary makes stored capital vulnerable to sudden disappearance; Proverbs pictures riches sprouting wings and flying off, turning possession into impermanence.

row.basis: Riches fail on the day of wrath
row.note: The commentary contrasts loss with deeds that carry a person through judgment; Proverbs says riches cannot deliver on the day of wrath but righteousness delivers from death.

row.basis: Borrowing without repayment
row.note: The commentary links debt to trust; the psalm contrasts a wicked borrower who does not repay with a righteous person who gives generously.

row.basis: Release of debts
row.note: The commentary develops debt as one face of truth; Deuteronomy commands release of loans at the appointed remission, connecting obligation to mercy within the community.

row.basis: Honest weights in trade
row.note: The commentary brings market trust and truthful judgment together; Proverbs condemns false scales and approves accurate weights in commerce.

row.basis: A general ban on swearing
row.note: The commentary’s witness scene uses an oath to establish a bequest; Jesus’ sermon tells disciples not to swear, giving a contrasting ethic for truthful speech.

row.basis: A house stands through rain and wind
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes ruined gardens with refuge; Jesus’ house on rock survives rain, floods, and wind because its builder acts on his words.

row.basis: A house collapses in the storm
row.note: The commentary calls the spider’s house an inadequate refuge and describes a storm ruining a garden; Jesus’ house built on sand falls when rain, flood, and wind strike.

row.basis: Trust as a spider’s web
row.note: The commentary makes the spider house a refuge that fails; Job says the confidence of the godless is like a spider’s web, matching the fragile shelter image.

row.basis: Spider webs cannot clothe
row.note: The commentary links the spider’s house to textile and failed protection; Isaiah says webs cannot serve as garments, making the woven product useless as covering.

row.basis: God as refuge and fortress
row.note: The commentary contrasts a spider’s false shelter with real security; the psalm names God as refuge and fortress, supplying a contrasting image of protection.

row.basis: Shelter from storm and heat
row.note: The commentary layers refuge with rain and tempest; Isaiah pictures a just ruler as shelter from wind and storm, a safe counterpart to the fragile garden or web.

row.basis: Ropes pull Jeremiah out of a pit
row.note: The commentary says a community is pulled back from an edge; Jeremiah is physically drawn from a cistern by ropes, a concrete rescue image with a different meaning from the shared covenant rope.

row.basis: A message sweet in the mouth and bitter inside
row.note: The commentary calls patience a bitter essence kept and passed on; John eats a scroll that tastes sweet and turns bitter in his stomach, making internalized truth costly.

row.basis: A received message must be spoken onward
row.note: The commentary ends with truth and patience changing hands; after eating the scroll, John is told to prophesy again to peoples and nations, connecting inward reception to transmission.

row.basis: A person sells all to gain hidden treasure
row.note: The commentary names buying error as a ruinous bargain; Jesus’ parable reverses the valuation, as a man sells what he has to gain a treasure worth more.

row.basis: Affliction produces endurance
row.note: The commentary imagines pressure and patience meeting; Paul says suffering produces endurance, interpreting hardship as a source of steadfastness rather than only loss.

row.basis: Faith and patience inherit promises
row.note: The commentary’s final community joins belief and patience; Hebrews says faith and patience characterize those who inherit the promises.

row.basis: A yoke and burden made light
row.note: The commentary defines the ascent through a burden and a freed neck; Jesus describes his own yoke as easy and burden as light, recasting burden as sustaining discipleship.

row.basis: Freedom from slavery’s yoke
row.note: The commentary makes freeing a captive the answer to the steep ascent; Paul says Christ set people free and warns them not to return to a yoke of slavery.

row.basis: Pressed but not crushed
row.note: The commentary opens with pressure that can destroy accumulated yield; Paul describes believers as hard pressed but not crushed, distinguishing pressure from final loss.

row.basis: Light affliction and a weight of glory
row.note: The commentary joins time’s pressure to scales and loss; Paul contrasts brief affliction with an eternal weight of glory, reversing the apparent measure of value.

row.basis: Good works stored as future treasure
row.note: The commentary makes righteous deeds the secure yield of mortal time; Timothy tells the rich to be rich in good works and store treasure for the future.

row.basis: This life as a vestibule before the next world
row.note: The commentary treats time as a limited span whose use determines what follows; Avot compares this world to a vestibule in which one prepares before entering the banquet hall.

row.basis: A will takes effect after death
row.note: The commentary’s bequest is activated by impending death; Hebrews’ next legal step says a will takes effect only after death, sharpening the contrast between present custody and later transfer.

row.basis: Joseph forgotten in confinement
row.note: The commentary pairs Joseph’s prison with patience; after the cupbearer is restored, he forgets Joseph, adding the concrete delay of being left confined and unremembered.

row.basis: Two years pass before Joseph is recalled
row.note: The commentary makes detention and patience meet; Genesis marks two full years before Pharaoh’s dream brings the imprisoned Joseph back into view, specifying the length of the wait.

row.basis: A dying patriarch asks for an oath about burial
row.note: The commentary’s testament scene joins approaching death, trust, and obligation; Jacob, near death, asks Joseph to swear that he will not bury him in Egypt.

row.basis: The deathbed request is secured by an oath
row.note: The commentary places oath and bequest together at death; Joseph swears to Jacob’s burial request, turning a dying person’s instruction into an entrusted duty.

row.basis: A final oath entrusted to the next generation
row.note: The commentary joins death, custody, and what passes between people; Joseph makes Israel’s descendants swear to carry his bones when God visits them.

row.basis: Fire consumes accumulated flocks and servants
row.note: The commentary’s ruined garden includes a destructive fiery storm; in Job’s sequence of calamities, fire from heaven consumes sheep and servants, one part of the sudden loss of his holdings.

row.basis: Numbering days to gain wisdom
row.note: The commentary treats time as expiring capital; the psalm asks to be taught to number one’s days so the heart may gain wisdom, turning limited time into a prompt for action.

row.basis: Meditating on instruction day and night
row.note: The commentary says communal counsel joins like night and day; the psalmist meditates on Torah day and night, making ethical instruction a sustained practice across time.

row.basis: A righteous tree bears fruit in season and does not wither
row.note: The commentary’s fruitful garden is destroyed at the moment of expected yield; Psalm 1 pictures the righteous as a watered tree whose seasonal fruit remains, a counter-image of stability.

row.basis: Summer fruit announces the end
row.note: The commentary layers ripe produce with life’s late hour and the end of time; Amos’s basket of summer fruit signals that Israel’s end has arrived, making harvest itself an omen of ending.

row.basis: Human growth fades while the word endures
row.note: The commentary moves from mortal time to truth that is transmitted and kept; Isaiah contrasts fading grass and flowers with the enduring word of God.

row.basis: Truth bound at the neck and written on the heart
row.note: The commentary joins truth to holding and binding; Proverbs tells the reader to bind faithfulness and truth around the neck and write them on the heart, combining tethering with inward preservation.

row.basis: A person becomes surety for a neighbor
row.note: The commentary gives patience the secondary image of a guarantor and joins trust to debt; Proverbs depicts someone pledging security for a neighbor, making the guarantee a concrete accepted burden.

row.basis: A pledged garment returned before sunset
row.note: The commentary joins debt, holding, and release within passing time; Exodus requires a creditor to return a poor borrower’s garment by sunset, so the pledge cannot become lasting captivity.

row.basis: A freed servant sent away with produce
row.note: The commentary defines the ascent through freeing a captive and feeding the hungry; Deuteronomy says not to send a released servant away empty-handed but to provide from flock, threshing floor, and winepress.

row.basis: A creditor threatens to take a widow’s sons as slaves
row.note: The commentary brings debt and release from captivity together; the widow’s unpaid debt puts her sons at risk of enslavement, making the financial obligation a threat to family freedom.

row.basis: Oil sold to pay debt and preserve a livelihood
row.note: The commentary’s debt and release scenes meet in Elisha’s instruction: the widow sells the multiplied oil, pays the creditor, and lives on what remains.

row.basis: Remember the one who stood as guarantor
row.note: The commentary calls patience a guarantor; Sirach warns not to forget the kindness of one who guaranteed a neighbor’s debt and risked much on that person’s behalf.

row.basis: Jesus as guarantor of a better covenant
row.note: The commentary’s secondary guarantor image meets Hebrews’ explicit description of Jesus as guarantor, applying financial surety language to the covenant.

row.basis: Truth heard, believed, and sealed
row.note: The commentary gathers belief, truth, and what is kept; Ephesians says its readers heard the word of truth, believed, and were sealed with the promised Spirit.

row.basis: A seal that guarantees inheritance
row.note: The commentary calls patience a guarantor and ends with what is preserved; Ephesians calls the Spirit the guarantee of inheritance until redemption.

row.basis: Patience expressed by bearing with one another
row.note: The commentary turns patience into reciprocal communal counsel; Paul joins humility, patience, and bearing with one another in love.

row.basis: Unity held by a bond of peace
row.note: The commentary pictures people holding together; Paul urges preservation of the Spirit’s unity through a bond of peace.

row.basis: Love rejoices with truth
row.note: The commentary makes truth the content of mutual counsel; Paul says love rejoices with the truth, placing truthful conduct inside communal ethics.

row.basis: Love bears and endures all things
row.note: The commentary presents patience as a quality exchanged within the community; Paul describes love as bearing and enduring all things, a sustained communal form of sabr.

row.basis: Patient persistence in good work
row.note: The commentary’s exception to loss joins belief, good deeds, and patience; Paul describes those who persist patiently in good work as seeking glory and eternal life.

row.basis: Daily mutual exhortation prevents hardening
row.note: The commentary’s community advises one another; Hebrews commands daily encouragement so that no one is hardened by sin’s deceit, specifying both the repeated action and its danger.

row.basis: Endurance after doing God’s will
row.note: The commentary closes with good action and patience held together; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God’s will in order to receive what is promised.

row.basis: Lay aside weight and run with endurance
row.note: The commentary makes the steep ascent a road with a load; Hebrews tells runners to lay aside every weight and run the set race with endurance.

row.basis: Good deeds as advocates and a shield
row.note: The commentary says deeds distinguish those who escape loss; Avot pictures a commandment as an advocate and repentance with good deeds as a shield against punishment.

row.basis: The word stored in the heart
row.note: The commentary ends with truth received and preserved; the psalmist stores God’s word in the heart as a safeguard against sin, making inward keeping an ethical act.

row.basis: Time treated as something to redeem
row.note: The commentary calls time capital that can be spent or lost; Paul urges believers to make the most of the time because the days are evil, giving time an explicit economic value.

row.basis: Ripe grapes cast into the winepress of judgment
row.note: The commentary layers fruit, pressing, and the end; Revelation gathers ripe grapes and casts them into God’s great winepress, making the press a harvest image of judgment.

row.basis: Steadfast work is not in vain
row.note: The commentary says most human effort is loss but closes with faithful work and patience; Paul calls believers steadfast and abundant in the Lord’s work, assuring them that such labor is not empty.

row.basis: One more year for a fruitless tree
row.note: The commentary overlaps orchard, aging time, and the risk of losing fruit; the gardener asks for one more year to tend the barren fig tree, making patience a limited extension before judgment.

row.basis: Truth as a means of release
row.note: The commentary joins truth to freeing a captive; Jesus says knowing the truth will make his hearers free, recasting liberation as an effect of truth.

row.basis: The word as fire and a rock-breaking hammer
row.note: The commentary gives truth the image of a straight blow; Jeremiah compares God’s word to fire and a hammer that breaks rock, making truthful speech forceful rather than merely abstract.

row.basis: A dying Jesus entrusts his mother
row.note: The commentary’s testament scene gathers approaching death, entrusted care, and a transfer between people; Jesus from the cross gives his mother and the beloved disciple to one another.

row.basis: The entrusted person is received into a home
row.note: The commentary says trust and custody meet at death; the disciple takes Mary into his own home, carrying out the deathbed entrustment as practical care.
